newsitem.title: UK: IT systems allow UK gas competition to start early.
newsitem.headline: IT systems allow UK gas competition to start early.

text.p: A breakthrough in the computer systems allowing UK domestic gas customers to transfer between suppliers is behind Monday's announcement by industry regulator Ofgas that full competition will start on November 1.

Ofgas announced that full competition in the domestic gas supply business will be introduced in six steps from November 1. On that date, 2.5 million customers in Scotland, Durham, Hartlepool, Middlesborough, Northumberland, Redcar and Cleveland, Stockton-on-Tees and Tyne and Wear will be able to buy gas from any licensed supplier.

The rest of Britain will open for competition in stages on 27 February 1998 (2.8 million customers in Yorkshire, Manchester and the north of England), 27 March (2.9 million customers in other areas of northern England), 24 April (3.2 million users in Wales and the West Midlands), 22 May (3.1 million users in most of the home counties around London) and 19 June (3.1 million users in the rest of the country, mainly in London and Surrey).

Under the original plan, the full roll out of competiton was not due to start until next year. But Transco, the pipeline arm of BG plc and Ofgas had long been working to introduce the roll out of domestic competition ahead of the coming winter.

There had been fears that Transco's domestic competition computer system, UK Link, would not be ready until next year. But Transco said in a statement that it has now developed an interim solution based on a new database which will allow roll-out to start in the specified area on November 1.
The system, it added, "will not jeopardise the development and testing of the systems required to support the entire market of 19 million gas customers."

The UK Link system is used to track consumers as they switch suppliers and to calculate the cost to the gas supplier of transporting gas from beach terminals to domestic meters. It contains Europe's third largest database, and concerns over whether it could be made to work on time have been central to the timetable for the introduction of full competition.
Ofgas' announcement is technically a consultation document listing a series of proposed starting dates for the different areas. The deadline for responses to the document is 24 July.

"This will be the world's biggest competitive domestic gas market, and I am grateful for the amount of work that staff at Transco and BGT (British Gas Trading, part of Centrica plc ) have put into the development of these proposals," said Clare Spottiswoode, Director General of Ofgas.

"These latest proposals will bring the benefits of competition to over 20 million customers throughout Great Britain," she added. She continued that customers in pilot areas trialling the system have already been able to reduce average gas bills of 325 stg a year by around 20 percent by switching supplier.
"This sort of saving will soon be available to everyone on mains gas," she said.
Sue Slipman, Director of the Gas Consumers Council (GCC), expressed concern that some "potential risks" be addressed before full competition roll-out starts.

"GCC want the earliest possible date for the opening up of domestic gas competition; but we want a guarantee of decent standards of service to consumers and a market that can bring benefits of competition to all consumers, including the most vulnerable," she said in a statement.

The south western counties of Devon, Somerset and Cornwall were opened to competition in April 1996 as a first pilot area. This was followed by a second pilot in Avon, Dorset, Kent and East and West Sussex in February and March this year. By the end of June, 377,136 customers of a total of around 2 million in these areas had switched between the 14 licensed suppliers, which include BGT.
Until April 1996, British Gas plc, now demerged into Centrica plc and BG plc, held a monopoly on the supply of gas to domestic consumers.
